young.html: William James was a Harvard professor who loved to settle arguments. One summer, on a camping trip, he found his friends in a hot dispute about a squirrel.

A squirrel clings to one side of a tree trunk. A man walks all the way around the tree to see it, but the squirrel keeps moving too, always staying on the far side. Did the man go "round" the squirrel? Half the campers said yes, half said no.

young.name: gb-james-squirrel
young.cap: Walk the man around the tree. Then switch between the two meanings of "going round" and see the answer change.

young.html: James said both sides were right: it depends on what you mean by "going round." If you mean north, east, south and west of the squirrel, yes. If you mean in front of it, then to its side, then behind it, no, because the squirrel always faced him. Once you ask "what difference does it make?", the quarrel goes away. That way of thinking is called pragmatism.

The difference test. Next time your family argues about a word ("Is a hot dog a sandwich?"), ask James's question: what would be different if one side were right? Is the argument about the world, or only about the word?

full.html: William James (1842–1910) was already famous for The Principles of Psychology (1890), on the 19th-century part of this ladder. In late 1906 and early 1907 he gave lectures in Boston and New York on a way of thinking his friend Charles Sanders Peirce had named pragmatism years before. They came out in 1907 as Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking, dedicated to the memory of John Stuart Mill.

James begins with temperament. Some thinkers are "tender-minded": they trust principles, hope for a unified and good world, and lean toward religion and free will. Others are "tough-minded": they trust facts, see many separate things, and lean toward materialism and doubt. James offers pragmatism as a way to keep the facts and still leave room for hope.
After the squirrel story James draws the lesson:

full.text: The pragmatic method is primarily a method of settling metaphysical disputes that otherwise might be interminable. Is the world one or many?—fated or free?—material or spiritual?—here are notions either of which may or may not hold good of the world; and disputes over such notions are unending.
full.author: William James
full.ed: Longmans, Green, and Co., New York

full.html: The method, in our words: ask what practical difference it would make if one idea were true rather than the other. If there is no difference at all, the dispute is idle. If there is a difference, now you know what you are really arguing about.

The most controversial lectures turn the method on truth itself. For James, an idea is not true by simply copying reality like a photograph. It becomes true as it guides us well through experience and holds up when we check it.

full.text: "Grant an idea or belief to be true," it says, "what concrete difference will its being true make in any one's actual life? How will the truth be realized? What experiences will be different from those which would obtain if the belief were false? What, in short, is the truth's cash-value in experiential terms?"
full.author: William James
full.ed: Longmans, Green, and Co., New York

full.text: True ideas are those that we can assimilate, validate, corroborate and verify. False ideas are those that we can not.
full.author: William James
full.ed: Longmans, Green, and Co., New York

full.html: Pragmatism was a sensation and a target. Bertrand Russell and G. E. Moore objected that if "true" meant "useful to believe," a false belief that made someone happy would count as true; James replied that he meant what works in the long run and against all the evidence, not comfort of the moment. Peirce, uneasy with James's version, renamed his own view "pragmaticism," a word he said was "ugly enough to be safe from kidnappers." John Dewey carried pragmatism into education and public life, and it is often called America's most distinctive philosophy. Philosophers still debate theories of truth; many who reject James's account keep his method of asking what difference a claim makes.
Reading "truth is what works" as "believe whatever is convenient." James insisted that a true idea must fit with facts, with our other beliefs, and with what later experience shows.

items: Mill's Utilitarianism judges actions by their results; James, who dedicated the book to Mill, judges ideas by theirs.
Hume and Berkeley asked what we mean by our words in terms of experience; James counts them as forerunners.
Dewey's Experience and Education, a later rung, applies pragmatist ideas to schooling.
Russell's Problems of Philosophy, the next rung, appeared five years later and took a very different view of truth.
Is a belief true because it works, or does it work because it is true?
Are some arguments only about words? How can you tell?
Can it be reasonable to believe something before all the evidence is in?
What is the difference between "useful" and "true"?

questions: So: did the man go round the squirrel? Explain both answers.
Think of a family argument that turned out to be about the meaning of a word.
Are you more tough-minded or tender-minded? Can a person be both?
James asked, "What difference would it make?" Try it on a question you have wondered about.
Can a belief make you happy and still be false? What would James say?
